Build a model that predicts **single-family sale prices in Chicago, 2023–2025**, using only the tools from this course. The file contains **only features of the house itself**. We return to both issues in Part 4. --- ## Part 2: Build the model Start with a structure-only baseline. Then add features in steps you can learn from, logging each one. Keep the log in a tibble with columns `model`, `added`, `cv_rmse`, `moran_i`, `notes`. ### Download the geographic and income data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} acs_cache <- "data/assignment5/acs_tracts_income_2023.rds" if (file.exists(acs_cache)) { acs_tracts <- readRDS(acs_cache) } else { acs_tracts <- get_acs( geography = "tract", state = "IL", county = "Cook", variables = c(income = "B19013_001"), year = 2023, survey = "acs5", output = "wide", geometry = TRUE, progress_bar = FALSE ) %>% st_transform(3435) saveRDS(acs_tracts, acs_cache) } income <- acs_tracts %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% select(GEOID, income = incomeE, income_moe = incomeM) %>% mutate(income = if_else(income > 0, income, NA_real_)) tracts <- acs_tracts %>% select(GEOID, NAME) ``` ::: ### Build the location features We join houses to Census tracts, calculate their distance from the Loop, and make three distance rings. The tract is a place category, like the district factor in Week 6. We use these location features without using other houses' prices. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} all_sales <- st_join( all_sales, tracts %>% select(tract = GEOID), join = st_intersects, left = TRUE ) %>% distinct(id, .keep_all = TRUE) %>% left_join(income, by = c("tract" = "GEOID")) all_sales %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(split) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}

We started with house characteristics, then added location because similar houses can sell for different prices across Chicago. We compared squared terms, log size, distance, rings, interactions and tract fixed effects. Adding tract-specific size slopes and an age-by-ring interaction gave the lowest CV RMSE among the tested formulas. We chose among them using the same grouped CV folds. These fitted relationships describe associations; they do not tell us what changing a house or neighborhood would cause. Our central-air coefficient is $17,524. As beta-hat, it is the estimated price difference between the supplied central-air categories, holding the other predictors fixed. For y-hat, switching that indicator from 0 to 1 changes the predicted price by that amount. We cannot interpret it as the return from installing air conditioning because condition and renovations may also differ between houses. We would not give this model to the Assessor for operational use yet. It improves on the baseline, but the residual maps and LISA results show where further checks are needed. Dollar RMSE can hide large proportional errors for inexpensive houses. Income-group comparisons help us describe that concern, but tract income is not an owner's income and cannot establish individual fairness. We removed bundled transactions rather than guessing how to divide their prices. We kept both price tails because we could not justify excluding them. Grouping rounded coordinates helps with repeated sales, but verified parcel IDs would be better. Our CV score also influenced model selection, so it is not an independent final test. Before using this model for assessments, we would evaluate a later year and held-out geographic areas, verify condition and transaction details, and investigate impossible predictions. We would follow Week 8's approach of checking residual clusters and measuring a plausible missing feature before adding it.
